name: a-aerial-wall-between
prompt: Photograph taken from very high above, camera pointing straight down at the ground, no horizon and no sky, the earth laid flat like a map in a tall vertical frame. One long pale concrete boundary wall crosses the whole frame from left edge to right edge just below the middle, ruler-straight and casting almost no shadow. Above the wall: a private gated compound of a dozen identical white flat-roofed villas set in a neat grid, each with its own rectangular swimming pool of bright turquoise water, clipped emerald lawns, a single curving driveway, no cars moving, no people anywhere, not a ripple on any pool. Below the wall, packed tight against its base without a single metre of gap: a crowded settlement of improvised shelters roofed in faded blue, grey and rust-coloured tarpaulin and corrugated sheet, narrow dirt lanes, washing strung between roofs, thin threads of grey smoke from cooking fires drifting sideways, people reduced to tiny specks of colour. Even, shadowless light from a thick white overcast, everything sharp from corner to corner, large-format documentary detail, dusty ochre, khaki and ash tones everywhere except the repeated hard blue rectangles of the pools. Calm, still and almost geometric, a composition that first reads as an abstract quilt of shapes and only then as two worlds divided. No text, no signs, no lettering, no logos anywhere. Thanks.

name: a-flash-banquet-left-standing
prompt: A vertical snapshot taken at night inside the private dining saloon of a vast luxury yacht, the kind of photo someone takes with a cheap point-and-shoot and its built-in flash fired straight ahead. The camera stands at the head of a very long banquet table at seated eye height and looks down its full length toward the dark end of the room. The table is still set for a feast that finished years ago: crumpled white linen gone grey, rows of champagne coupes and tall flutes coated in a fur of pale dust, a silver platter holding a shallow puddle and a few rounded lumps where an ice swan once stood, half-eaten towers of fruit dried to brown husks, a toppled candelabra, napkins dropped on the carpet. Gilded chairs with crimson velvet seats are shoved back at odd angles and one lies on its side, as if the whole party stood up at once and walked out. The flash blasts the foreground in flat bright white, makes the gold leaf and crystal glare, and throws hard black shadows of the chairs and glasses onto the lacquered walls; everything past the middle of the table falls off fast into murk. Behind the far end, a wall of floor-to-ceiling glass shows only pitch-black water and sky, broken by three or four small orange fires burning along a distant shoreline. Saturated, slightly cheap colour: hot reds, brassy gold, sickly green tint in the shadows, a touch of film grain. No people anywhere. Bottles and plates carry no labels, no text, no signs or lettering in the frame. Funny, gaudy and quietly mournful at the same time. Thanks.

name: a-painted-bored-suburb
prompt: A digitally painted illustration with visible soft brushwork and a gouache-like matte finish, portrait frame. A quiet two-lane country road runs straight away from the viewer through a sleepy Nordic housing estate of low timber houses, hedges and a leaning lamp post, at late-afternoon golden hour. In the lower foreground, seen from behind and slightly to one side, a ten-year-old child in a padded jacket sits astride a small bicycle with one foot on the tarmac, shoulders slumped, head tipped toward the empty verge, plainly bored. Halfway down the road a makeshift barrier of planks, painted in faded red and white stripes and propped on trestles, closes the way. Beyond the rooftops, filling the upper half of the frame, a range of colossal windowless data halls and three cooling towers stand dark and cold, their flat grey walls stained by rain, chain-link fences swallowed by waist-high wild grass and birch saplings; nothing moves, no steam, no lights. Camera at the child's eye height, wide lens, deep focus, the vast buildings softened by atmospheric haze so their size reads through distance. Warm honey and amber light rakes across the foreground and throws long shadows up the road, while the distance falls into pale slate blue and lavender. Muted, quiet palette, gentle dust in the air, every surface plain and unmarked. The feeling of a place years after the catastrophe, where the ruins have become ordinary scenery and nobody looks at them any more.

name: a-kerbside-furniture-deadpan
prompt: Upright colour photograph made on a large-format view camera standing on its tripod in the exact middle of an empty residential road at midday, lens dead level, both kerbs running away in perfect symmetry towards one vanishing point. Either side, a long unbroken row of matching two-up two-down red-brick terraces with grey slate roofs and paired chimney stacks. Along the pavement, outside each house, that household's whole life has been carried out and left: a floral settee, a child's white cot with the mattress still in it, a fridge-freezer with brown tape across its door, dining chairs stacked upside down, a standard lamp, a telly, swollen cardboard boxes darkened by a passing shower, black bin bags, photographs in frames turned face down on a chest of drawers. The pile is repeated, near identical, at every house down to the far end of the road, as though the bailiffs came for the entire street on one morning. Each front door and downstairs window is sealed with a new sheet of pale unpainted plywood, screwed in tight; house numbers, letterboxes and lettering are all absent. Wet tarmac, no parked cars, no people, no birds. Overcast noon, a blank milky sky giving soft even light with no shadows and no mood. Deep focus, crisp from the kerbstones nearest the lens to the chimney pots at the horizon, fine film grain, quiet natural colour: brick red, wet slate, beige and cream upholstery, the yellow of fresh plywood marching away in rhythm. A neutral, patient, deadpan record, as plain as an estate agent's survey; the stillness carries it.

name: b-grey-tableau-office
prompt: Vertical portrait shot of a cramped, almost empty council waiting office, seen square-on and dead level from the eye height of someone sitting down, the camera locked off at the far wall so the whole room reads like a stage set built in front of the lens. Exactly on the centre line, one figure sits bolt upright behind a small bare municipal desk of pale laminate on thin steel legs, visible head to shoes beneath the desk. The figure wears a plain charcoal knitted ski mask covering the whole head and neck, a dull grey-green office jacket buttoned to the collar, and dark wool gloves; the gloved hands lie folded one over the other on the empty desktop. On the mask, circling only the wearer's left eye hole, sits a thin crisp white ring, and inside it, at roughly two o'clock, a small red triangle with softened corners pointing downward. The eyes in the holes hold the lens steadily, calm and courteous, as if about to apologise for a very long delay. Behind, a blank wall in washed-out sage, a round white clock whose face has no hands at all, and in one corner a rubber plant in a beige pot, its leaves sagging toward the lino. Beside the desk, a single moulded plastic visitor chair stands empty, turned toward the figure. Speckled grey linoleum underfoot. Everything is sharp from the desk's front edge to the back wall, as through a moderately wide 35mm lens with no distortion. Light is perfectly even and shadowless, a pale overcast glow from ceiling panels with no visible source, leaving skin-pale surfaces, no highlights and no dark corners anywhere. Colours are drained and chalky: putty grey, faded mint, dusty olive, beige, off-white; the one saturated note is the small red triangle. Still, faintly ridiculous and quietly sad, like a polite interview that has already gone badly. No text, signs, posters, labels or lettering anywhere. Thanks.

name: b-fireside-public-information
prompt: Vertical frame lifted from a government advice film broadcast on a 1970s television evening, captured on punchy, contrasty 16mm colour reversal stock with heavy visible grain and slightly smeared telecine sharpness. A masked presenter sits squarely in a deep winged armchair covered in tobacco-brown corduroy, centred in a cramped front parlour at night. The wall behind is papered with large repeating hexagons and loops in tangerine, ochre and dark cocoa on a cream ground. A floor lamp with a fringed drum shade stands just off the chair's right ear, its bulb making a warm amber pool over the sitter's shoulders while the room's edges sink into murky umber. Beside the chair, on a low teak occasional table, a bone-china teacup and saucer sit on a crocheted white mat, a curl of steam rising. The presenter's whole head is hidden in a dark navy knitted balaclava with ribbed stitching, only the eyes showing through two holes; encircling the hole of the wearer's left eye is a fine white outline loop, and set within that loop near its upper right, the two o'clock position, a tiny scarlet triangular patch whose three tips are blunted, one tip aimed at the floor. Hands in black leather gloves lie relaxed along both wooden-capped armrests. Framed from the sternum to just above the crown, lens at the sitter's eye height, the gaze fixed directly into camera with the polite, unhurried calm of a man about to talk the nation through its gas bill. Faintly soft focus, saturated oranges and reds against milky faded highlights, inky shadows, a soft darkening falloff around the frame's corners, a speck of dust or two on the emulsion. No writing, captions or lettering anywhere in the picture. Thanks.

name: b-flash-doorstep-closeup
prompt: Vertical night snapshot taken from barely an arm's length away on a dark porch: a masked visitor's head and shoulders crowd the picture almost edge to edge, caught by one bare speedlight mounted on a bracket right above a short wide lens, so the hard shadow drops straight down behind the neck. The visitor wears an ordinary black wool ski mask, the knit so close and so sharply lit that each twisted strand, bobble and loose hair of yarn reads clearly. Stitched round the eye opening on the wearer's own left (picture right) is a slim white circle; tucked within it, up toward the 2 o'clock position, a tiny crimson triangle, corners rounded off, tip aimed at the ground. Both marks bounce the flash back hot and bright. Behind the mask the gaze holds the lens dead level, steady, unblinking, the patient calm of a well-mannered caller who has already seen how the evening turns out. Low in the corner, a hand in a black glove lifts just above the shoulder line in a modest little wave. Exposure is pushed: the centre of the face glows nearly white, colours run rich and punchy, then the light dies quickly into inky darkness, leaving only a sliver of glossy painted door jamb and the small lit circle of a doorbell floating in the black. Crisp, raw, slightly vignetted, no blur, no writing, numbers or symbols beyond the two marks on the mask. Thanks.

name: b-standing-in-the-drained-pool
prompt: Portrait-format photograph made from the bottom of the shallow end of a long, waterless private pool, aimed straight along its length to the deep end; a 28mm lens held at chest height, so the tiled floor tilts away and climbs toward the far wall, perfect left-right symmetry, deep focus with every tile and window crisp. Years without water: sun-bleached turquoise mosaic crazed with hairline cracks and grimy rings where the waterline used to sit, a heap of dry brown leaves banked around the drain grate, one white resin sun lounger tipped on its side with a leg snapped clean off. Dead centre at the lowest point of the deep end stands a single figure, upright and patient, facing the lens with mild, courteous attention, black leather gloved hands folded behind the back the way a museum guide waits for stragglers. A plain black ribbed-wool ski mask covers the whole head with no skin showing; a slim white circle is stitched around the left eye opening (the wearer's left), and inside that circle, toward its upper right at roughly the two o'clock position, sits a small downward-pointing red triangle with softened corners. Charcoal wool overcoat fastened high, grey slacks, plain shoes. Rising over the pool's edge and filling the top of the frame, the abandoned villa: flaking cream plaster, shutters closed, an empty terrace with one withered potted palm. Even white overcast sky, soft light with no shadows. Chalky, faded colours of bone, pale aqua, ash and leaf-brown, the red triangle the only bright note. Utterly still, formal, quietly ridiculous. No water, nobody else, no lettering, numbers or depth markers anywhere.

name: c-blue-hour-empty-horizon
prompt: Upright portrait seascape at blue hour, some twenty minutes after the sun has gone, shot from a tripod set low beside a sheltered bay at high tide so no rocks or sand intrude. A three-minute exposure has ironed the water into a single seamless pane of dusky steel blue, occupying just the bottom fifth of the picture and softly echoing the sky above it. Along that low, dead-level horizon runs a hairline of far-off coast, a flat charcoal strip with no visible detail, and on it one tiny warm glow, like a porch lamp miles away, which drops a faint thread of gold down across the still water. Above, nothing but sky: an enormous, perfectly smooth gradient that starts as deep indigo near the top edge, eases through royal blue and soft lavender, and ends in a narrow, gentle peach glow resting on the coastline. Cloudless, birdless, no boats, no stars, no lens flare; the upper and central areas stay completely empty and calm, ready to hold a mark added later. Standard focal length, everything sharp, low contrast, clean shadows, a cool hushed palette broken by that single ember of warmth. The mood is the first peaceful dusk after a long disaster: quiet, unhurried, faintly hopeful. Keep it wordless, with no writing, symbols or printed marks on anything.
